metadata.title: Sinkhorn Distances: Lightspeed Computation of Optimal Transportation Distances

eq:pen.section: Computing Sinkhorn Distances with the Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm

nodes.name: Frobenius dot-product
nodes.statement: In what follows, $\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle$ stands for the Frobenius dot-product.

nodes.name: Transportation polytope
nodes.statement: For two histograms $r$ and $c$ in the simplex $\Sigma_d\defeq \{x\in \RR^d_+: x^T\ones_d=1\}$, we write $U(r,c)$ for the transportation polytope of $r$ and $c$, namely the polyhedral set of $d\times d$ matrices: $$U(r,c)\defeq \{P\in\RR_+^{d\times d}\; |\; P\ones_d=r, P^T\ones_d=c\},$$ where $\ones_d$ is the $d$ dimensional vector of ones.
nodes.genus: the polyhedral set of $d\times d$ matrices
nodes.statement_short: The simplex $\Sigma_d$ of histograms and the transportation polytope $U(r,c)$ of nonnegative matrices with row sums $r$ and column sums $c$.

nodes.name: Probabilistic interpretation of the transportation polytope
nodes.statement: $U(r,c)$ contains all nonnegative $d\times d$ matrices with row and column sums $r$ and $c$ respectively. $U(r,c)$ has a probabilistic interpretation: for $X$ and $Y$ two multinomial random variables taking values in $\{1,\cdots,d\}$, each with distribution $r$ and $c$ respectively, the set $U(r,c)$ contains all possible \emph{joint probabilities} of $(X,Y)$. Indeed, any matrix $P\in U(r,c)$ can be identified with a joint probability for $(X,Y)$ such that $p(X=i,Y=j)=p_{ij}$. Such joint probabilities are also known as \emph{contingency tables}.
nodes.statement_short: Matrices in $U(r,c)$ are the joint probabilities (contingency tables) of two variables with marginals $r$ and $c$.

nodes.name: Entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence of tables
nodes.statement: We define the entropy $h$ and the Kullback-Leibler divergences of these tables and their marginals as \begin{gather*} r\in\Sigma_d,\quad h(r)=-\sum_{i=1}^d r_i \log r_i,\quad \quad P\in U(r,c),\quad h(P)=-\sum_{i,j=1}^d p_{ij} \log p_{ij}\\ P,Q \in U(r,c),\quad \mathbf{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_{ij}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}. \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Shannon entropy of histograms and tables and the KL divergence between tables.

nodes.name: Optimal transportation problem
nodes.statement: Given a $d\times d$ cost matrix $M$, the cost of mapping $r$ to $c$ using a transportation matrix (or joint probability) $P$ can be quantified as $\dotprod{P}{M}$. The following problem: $$ d_M(r,c) \defeq \min_{P\in U(r,c)} \dotprod{P}{M}. $$ is called an \emph{optimal transportation} problem between $r$ and $c$ given cost $M$.
nodes.statement_short: $d_M(r,c)$: minimize the cost $\langle P,M\rangle$ over the transportation polytope $U(r,c)$.

nodes.name: Optimal transportation distance is a metric
nodes.statement: The optimum of this problem, $d_M(r,c)$, is a distance~\citep[\S6.1]{villani09} whenever the matrix $M$ is itself a metric matrix, namely whenever $M$ belongs to the cone of distance matrices~\citep{avis1980extreme,brickell2008metric}: $$\Mcal=\{M\in\RR^{d\times d}_+:\forall i\leq d, m_{ii}=0;\, \forall i,j,k\leq d, m_{ij}\leq m_{ik} + m_{kj}\}.$$
assumptions: whenever the matrix $M$ is itself a metric matrix, namely whenever $M$ belongs to the cone of distance matrices
conclusions: The optimum of this problem, $d_M(r,c)$, is a distance
nodes.statement_short: $d_M$ is a distance whenever $M$ lies in the cone $\mathcal{M}$ of distance matrices.

nodes.name: Complexity of optimal transportation
nodes.statement: For a general matrix $M$, the worst case complexity of computing that optimum with any of the algorithms known so far scales in $O(d^3\log d)$ and turns out to be super-cubic in practice as well~\citep[\S2.1]{Pele-iccv2009}.

nodes.name: Basic information-theoretic entropy inequality
nodes.statement: \forall r,c \in \Sigma_d, \forall P\in U(r,c), h(P) \leq h(r)+h(c).
nodes.statement_short: The entropy of a joint table is at most the sum of the entropies of its marginals.
nodes.label: eq:basic

nodes.name: Tightness at the independence table
nodes.statement: This bound is tight, since the table $rc^T$ -- known as the independence table~\citep{good1963maximum} -- has an entropy of $h(rc^T)=h(r)+h(c)$.
conclusions: This bound is tight
nodes.statement_short: The independence table $rc^T$ attains the entropy bound.

nodes.name: Entropic transportation polytope $U_\alpha(r,c)$
nodes.statement: By the concavity of entropy, we can introduce the convex set $U_\alpha(r,c)\subset U(r,c)$ as $$U_\alpha(r,c)\defeq \{P\in U(r,c)\,|\,\mathbf{KL}(P\|rc^T)\leq \alpha \} = \{P\in U(r,c)\,|\, h(P)\geq h(r)+h(c)-\alpha\}$$
nodes.statement_short: $U_\alpha(r,c)$: tables in $U(r,c)$ within KL $\alpha$ of the independence table, i.e. with sufficient entropy.

nodes.name: Equivalence of the KL and entropy forms of $U_\alpha$
nodes.statement: These definitions are indeed equivalent, since one can easily check that $$\mathbf{KL}(P\|rc^T)= h(r)+h(c)-h(P),$$ a quantity which is also the mutual information $I(X\|Y)$ of two random variables $(X,Y)$ should they follow the joint probability $P$~\cite[\S2]{cover91elements}.
conclusions: These definitions are indeed equivalent
$$\mathbf{KL}(P\|rc^T)= h(r)+h(c)-h(P),$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{KL}(P\|rc^T)=h(r)+h(c)-h(P)$, the mutual information, so the two descriptions of $U_\alpha$ agree.

nodes.name: Optimal transport plans are vertices of the transportation polytope
nodes.statement: As a classic result of linear optimization, the optimum of classical optimal transportation distances is achieved on vertices of $U(r,c)$, that is $d\times d$ matrices with only up to $2d-1$ non-zero elements~\citep[\S8.1.3]{brualdi2006combinatorial}.
conclusions: the optimum of classical optimal transportation distances is achieved on vertices of $U(r,c)$, that is $d\times d$ matrices with only up to $2d-1$ non-zero elements
nodes.statement_short: Classical OT optima are attained at vertices of $U(r,c)$, with at most $2d-1$ nonzero entries.

nodes.name: Entropic smoothing gives a more robust distance
nodes.statement: Such plans can be interpreted as quasi-deterministic joint probabilities, since if $p_{ij}>0$, then very few values $p_{ij'}$ will have a non-zero probability. By mitigating the transportation cost objective with an entropic constraint, which is equivalent to following the max-entropy principle~\citep{PhysRev.106.620,dudik2006maximum} and thus for a given level of the cost look for the most smooth joint probability, we argue that we can provide a more robust notion of distance between histograms. Indeed, for a given pair $(r,c)$, finding plausible transportation plans with low cost (where plausibility is measured by entropy) is more informative than finding \emph{extreme plans} that are extremely unlikely to appear in nature.
nodes.statement_short: Vertex plans are quasi-deterministic; an entropic constraint selects smoother, more plausible plans and a more robust distance.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn Distances
nodes.statement: $\displaystyle d_{M,\alpha}(r,c)\defeq\min_{P\in U_\alpha(r,c)}\dotprod{P}{M}$
nodes.statement_short: $d_{M,\alpha}$: the optimal transport cost restricted to tables in $U_\alpha(r,c)$.
nodes.label: def:sinkhorn

nodes.name: Property 1 (large alpha recovers the transportation distance)
nodes.statement: For $\alpha$ large enough, the Sinkhorn distance $d_{M,\alpha}$ is the transportation distance $d_{M}$.
conclusions: the Sinkhorn distance $d_{M,\alpha}$ is the transportation distance $d_{M}$
nodes.label: prop:nsd

nodes.name: Proof of Property 1
nodes.statement: Since for any $P\in U(r,c), h(P)$ is lower bounded by $\tfrac{1}{2}(h(r)+h(c))$, we have that for $t$ large enough $U_{t}(r,c)= U(r,c)$ and thus both quantities coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Entropy lower bound implies $U_t(r,c)=U(r,c)$ for large $t$.

nodes.name: Independence Kernel
nodes.statement: When $\alpha=0$ and $M$ is a Euclidean Distance Matrix\footnote{$\exists n, \exists \varphi_1,\cdots,\varphi_d\in\RR^n$ such that $m_{ij}=\norm{\varphi_i - \varphi_j}_2^2$ \citep[\S5]{dattorro2005convex}. Recall that, in that case, $M.^t=[m_{ij}^t]$, $0<t<1$ is also a Euclidean distance matrix~\cite[p.78,\S3.2.10]{berg84harmonic} }, the Sinkhorn distance has the explicit form $d_{M,0}=r^T M c$. $d_{M,0}$ is a negative definite kernel, \ie\, $e^{-t r^TMc}$ is a positive definite kernel $\forall t>0$. We call this kernel the independence kernel.
assumptions: When $\alpha=0$ and $M$ is a Euclidean Distance Matrix
conclusions: the Sinkhorn distance has the explicit form $d_{M,0}=r^T M c$
$d_{M,0}$ is a negative definite kernel, \ie\, $e^{-t r^TMc}$ is a positive definite kernel $\forall t>0$
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha=0$ and Euclidean $M$, $d_{M,0}=r^TMc$ is negative definite, giving the positive definite independence kernel.

nodes.name: Coincidence axiom fails for small alpha
nodes.statement: Since for $\alpha$ small enough $d_{M,\alpha}(r,r)>0$ for any $r$ such that $h(r)>0$, Sinkhorn distances cannot satisfy the \emph{coincidence axiom}\footnote{satisfied if $d(x,y)=0\Leftrightarrow x=y$ holds for all $x,y$}. However, multiplying $d_{M,\alpha}$ by $\ones_{r\ne c}$ suffices to recover the coincidence property if needed.
nodes.statement_short: $d_{M,\alpha}(r,r)>0$ for small $\alpha$, so coincidence fails; multiplying by $\mathbf{1}_{r\ne c}$ restores it.

nodes.name: Metric properties of Sinkhorn distances
nodes.statement: For all $\alpha\geq 0$ and $M\in\Mcal$, $d_{M,\alpha}$ is symmetric and satisfies all triangle inequalities. The function $(r,c)\mapsto \ones_{r\ne c} d_{M,\alpha}(r,c)$ satisfies all three distance axioms.
conclusions: $d_{M,\alpha}$ is symmetric and satisfies all triangle inequalities
The function $(r,c)\mapsto \ones_{r\ne c} d_{M,\alpha}(r,c)$ satisfies all three distance axioms
nodes.statement_short: For metric $M$, $d_{M,\alpha}$ is symmetric with triangle inequality, and $\mathbf{1}_{r\ne c}d_{M,\alpha}$ is a distance.
nodes.label: theo:metric

nodes.name: Gluing Lemma With Entropic Constraint
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha\geq 0$ and $x,y,z$ be three elements of $\Sigma_d$. Let $P\in U_\alpha(x,y)$ and $Q\in U_\alpha(y,z)$ be two joint probabilities in the transportation polytopes of $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ with sufficient entropy. Let $S$ be the $d\times d$ matrix whose $(i,k)$'s coefficient is $s_{ik}\defeq \sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j}$. Then $S\in U_{\alpha}(x,z)$.
assumptions: Let $\alpha\geq 0$ and $x,y,z$ be three elements of $\Sigma_d$.
Let $P\in U_\alpha(x,y)$ and $Q\in U_\alpha(y,z)$ be two joint probabilities in the transportation polytopes of $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ with sufficient entropy.
Let $S$ be the $d\times d$ matrix whose $(i,k)$'s coefficient is $s_{ik}\defeq \sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j}$.
conclusions: Then $S\in U_{\alpha}(x,z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Gluing $P\in U_\alpha(x,y)$ and $Q\in U_\alpha(y,z)$ through $y$ gives a table in $U_\alpha(x,z)$.
nodes.label: lem:gluing

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: The symmetry of $d_{M,\alpha}$ is a direct result of $M$'s symmetry. Let $x,y,z$ be three elements in $\Sigma_d$. Let $P\in U_{\alpha}(x,y)$ and $Q\in U_{\alpha}(y,z)$ be the optimal solutions obtained when computing $d_{M,\alpha}(x,y)$ and $d_{M,\alpha}(y,z)$ respectively. Using the matrix $S$ of $U_{\alpha}(x,z)$ provided in Lemma~\ref{lem:gluing}, we proceed with the following chain of inequalities: $$\begin{aligned} d_{M,\alpha}(x,z)&=\min_{P\in U_\alpha(x,z)}\dotprod{X}{M} \leq \dotprod{S}{M} = \sum_{ik} m_{ik}\sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} \\ & \leq \sum_{ijk} \left(m_{ij}+m_{jk}\right) \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} = \sum_{ijk} m_{ij} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} +m_{jk} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} \\ & =\sum_{ij} m_{ij}p_{ij} \sum_k \frac{q_{jk}}{y_j} + \sum_{jk} m_{jk} q_{jk} \sum_i \frac{p_{ij}}{y_j}\\ &= \sum_{ij} m_{ij}p_{ij} + \sum_{jk} m_{jk} q_{jk} = d_{M,\alpha}(x,y)+d_{M,\alpha}(y,z).\,\blacksquare
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry from that of $M$; triangle inequality by gluing the two optimal plans with Lemma 1 and using the triangle inequality of $M$.

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: The symmetry of $d_{M,\alpha}$ is a direct result of $M$'s symmetry.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry follows from symmetry of $M$.

nodes.name: Optimal plans
nodes.statement: Let $x,y,z$ be three elements in $\Sigma_d$. Let $P\in U_{\alpha}(x,y)$ and $Q\in U_{\alpha}(y,z)$ be the optimal solutions obtained when computing $d_{M,\alpha}(x,y)$ and $d_{M,\alpha}(y,z)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $x,y,z$ and the optimal plans $P,Q$.

nodes.name: Glue and chain inequalities
nodes.statement: Using the matrix $S$ of $U_{\alpha}(x,z)$ provided in Lemma~\ref{lem:gluing}, we proceed with the following chain of inequalities: $$\begin{aligned} d_{M,\alpha}(x,z)&=\min_{P\in U_\alpha(x,z)}\dotprod{X}{M} \leq \dotprod{S}{M} = \sum_{ik} m_{ik}\sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} \\ & \leq \sum_{ijk} \left(m_{ij}+m_{jk}\right) \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} = \sum_{ijk} m_{ij} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} +m_{jk} \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j} \\ & =\sum_{ij} m_{ij}p_{ij} \sum_k \frac{q_{jk}}{y_j} + \sum_{jk} m_{jk} q_{jk} \sum_i \frac{p_{ij}}{y_j}\\ &= \sum_{ij} m_{ij}p_{ij} + \sum_{jk} m_{jk} q_{jk} = d_{M,\alpha}(x,y)+d_{M,\alpha}(y,z).\,\blacksquare
nodes.statement_short: Glue via Lemma 1 and bound the cost by a chain of inequalities.

nodes.name: Dual-Sinkhorn divergence (entropy-penalized transport)
nodes.statement: \boxed{d_{M}^{\lambda}(r,c) \defeq \dotprod{P^\lambda}{M},\,\text{ where } P^\lambda=\argmin_{P\in U(r,c)} \dotprod{P}{M} - \frac{1}{\lambda} h(P).}
nodes.section: 4 Computing Sinkhorn Distances with the Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: $d_M^\lambda$ is the cost of the minimizer of $\langle P,M\rangle-\frac1\lambda h(P)$ over $U(r,c)$.
nodes.label: eq:pen

nodes.name: Duality between alpha and lambda
nodes.statement: By duality theory we have that for every pair $(r,c)$, to each $\alpha$ corresponds an $\lambda\in[0,\infty]$ such that $d_{M,\alpha(r,c)}=d_{M}^{\lambda}(r,c)$.
nodes.section: 4 Computing Sinkhorn Distances with the Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm
conclusions: to each $\alpha$ corresponds an $\lambda\in[0,\infty]$ such that $d_{M,\alpha(r,c)}=d_{M}^{\lambda}(r,c)$
nodes.statement_short: Each constraint level $\alpha$ corresponds to a multiplier $\lambda$ with equal values.

nodes.name: Dual-Sinkhorn divergence
nodes.statement: We call $d_{M}^\lambda$ the dual-Sinkhorn divergence and show that it can be computed at a much cheaper cost than the classical optimal transportation problem for reasonable values of $\lambda$.
nodes.section: 4 Computing Sinkhorn Distances with the Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the entropic optimum
nodes.statement: When $\lambda>0$, the solution $P^\lambda$ is unique by strict convexity of minus the entropy.
conclusions: the solution $P^\lambda$ is unique

nodes.name: Scaling form of the entropic optimum
nodes.statement: In fact, $P^\lambda$ is necessarily of the form $u_i e^{-\lambda m_{ij}} v_j$, where $u$ and $v$ are two non-negative vectors uniquely defined up to a multiplicative factor.
conclusions: $P^\lambda$ is necessarily of the form $u_i e^{-\lambda m_{ij}} v_j$, where $u$ and $v$ are two non-negative vectors uniquely defined up to a multiplicative factor
nodes.statement_short: $P^\lambda_{ij}=u_i e^{-\lambda m_{ij}} v_j$ for nonnegative scaling vectors $u,v$.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn-Knopp fixed point iteration for $d^\lambda_M$
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithmic} \caption{Computation of $d^\lambda_M(r,c)$ using Sinkhorn-Knopp's fixed point iteration} \STATE \textbf{Input} \texttt{M}, $\lambda$, \texttt{r}, \texttt{c}. \STATE \texttt{I=(r>0); r=r(I); M=M(I,:); \texttt{K=exp(-$\lambda$*M)}} \STATE Set \texttt{x}=\texttt{ones(length(r),size(c,2))/length(r)}; \WHILE{\texttt{x} changes} \STATE \texttt{x=diag(1./r)*K*(c.*(1./(K'*(1./x))))} \ENDWHILE \STATE \texttt{u=1./x; v=c.*(1./(K'*u))} \STATE $d_{M}^\lambda$(\texttt{r},\texttt{c})=\texttt{sum(u.*((K.*M)*v))} \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Computes $d_M^\lambda(r,c)$ by alternately rescaling $K=e^{-\lambda M}$ to match marginals $r$ and $c$ (Sinkhorn-Knopp), vectorized over many $c$.

nodes.name: Restrict support and form K
nodes.statement: \texttt{I=(r>0); r=r(I); M=M(I,:); \texttt{K=exp(-$\lambda$*M)}}
nodes.statement_short: Drop zero entries of $r$ and form $K=e^{-\lambda M}$.

nodes.name: Initialize x
nodes.statement: Set \texttt{x}=\texttt{ones(length(r),size(c,2))/length(r)};
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the scaling vector uniformly.

nodes.name: Fixed-point loop
nodes.statement:
\WHILE{\texttt{x} changes}
		  \STATE \texttt{x=diag(1./r)*K*(c.*(1./(K'*(1./x))))}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate until x stops changing.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn update
nodes.statement_short: One Sinkhorn-Knopp fixed-point update of x.

nodes.name: Scaling vectors
nodes.statement_short: Recover scaling vectors u and v.

nodes.name: Distance
nodes.statement: $d_{M}^\lambda$(\texttt{r},\texttt{c})=\texttt{sum(u.*((K.*M)*v))}
nodes.statement_short: Return $d_M^\lambda=u^T(K\odot M)v$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the scaling form via the Lagrangian
nodes.statement: This well known fact in transportation theory~\citep{erlander1990gravity} can be indeed checked by forming the Lagrangian $\Lcal(P,\alpha,\beta)$ of the objective of Equation~\eqref{eq:pen} using $\alpha,\beta\geq \mathbf{0}_d$ for each of the two equality constraints in $U(r,c)$. For these two cost vectors $\alpha,\beta$, $$\Lcal(P,\alpha,\beta)=\sum_{ij} \frac{1}{\lambda}p_{ij}\log p_{ij}+ p_{ij}m_{ij} + \alpha^T(P \ones_d-r) + \beta^T(P^T\ones_d-c)$$ We obtain then, for any couple $(i,j)$, that if $\frac{\partial \Lcal}{\partial p_{ij}^\lambda}=0$, then $$ p_{ij}^\lambda= e^{-\frac{1}{2}-\lambda \alpha_i} e^{-\lambda m_{ij}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}-\lambda \beta_j}, $$ and thus recover the form provided above.
nodes.statement_short: Set the gradient of the Lagrangian of the penalized problem to zero to obtain the scaling form.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn's theorem
nodes.statement: \exists u,v>\mathbf{0}_d : P^\lambda = \diag(u) e^{-\lambda M} \diag(v).
conclusions: \exists u,v>\mathbf{0}_d : P^\lambda = \diag(u) e^{-\lambda M} \diag(v).
nodes.statement_short: $P^\lambda$ is the unique matrix of the form $\mathrm{diag}(u)e^{-\lambda M}\mathrm{diag}(v)$ with marginals $r,c$.
nodes.label: eq:sinkhorn

nodes.name: Vectorization of the algorithm
nodes.statement: Note that Algorithm~\ref{alg:sk} is \emph{vectorized}: it can be used as such to compute the distance between $r$ and a \emph{family of histograms} $C=[c_1,\cdots,c_N]$ by replacing $c$ with $C$. These $O(d^2N)$ linear algebra operations can be very quickly executed by using a GPGPU.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $c$ by a matrix $C$ computes distances to $N$ histograms at once in $O(d^2N)$ GPU-friendly operations.

nodes.name: Bisection search for $d_{M,\alpha}$
nodes.statement: With a naive approach, $d_{M,\alpha}$ can be obtained by computing $d_{M}^\lambda$ iteratively until the entropy of the solution $P^\lambda$ has reached an adequate value $h(r)+h(c)-\alpha$. Since the entropy of $P^\lambda$ decreases monotonically when $\lambda$ increases, this search can be carried out by simple bisection, starting with a small $\lambda$ which is iteratively increased.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $d_{M,\alpha}$ by computing $d_M^\lambda$ and bisecting on $\lambda$ until the entropy of $P^\lambda$ reaches $h(r)+h(c)-\alpha$.

nodes.name: Compute dual-Sinkhorn
nodes.statement: computing $d_{M}^\lambda$ iteratively
nodes.statement_short: Compute $d_M^\lambda$ for the current $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Entropy target
nodes.statement: until the entropy of the solution $P^\lambda$ has reached an adequate value $h(r)+h(c)-\alpha$
nodes.statement_short: Stop when $h(P^\lambda)$ reaches $h(r)+h(c)-\alpha$.

nodes.name: Bisection on lambda
nodes.statement: this search can be carried out by simple bisection, starting with a small $\lambda$ which is iteratively increased
nodes.statement_short: Adjust $\lambda$ by bisection, starting small and increasing.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn distance (as $d_M^\lambda$)
nodes.statement: In the rest of this paper we will now refer to $d_{M}^\lambda$ as the Sinkhorn distance, despite the fact that it is not provably a distance.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn distance outperforms other distances on MNIST
nodes.statement: The Sinkhorn distance beats by a safe margin all other distances, including the EMD.
conclusions: The Sinkhorn distance beats by a safe margin all other distances, including the EMD.

nodes.name: Dual-Sinkhorn divergence exceeds the EMD
nodes.statement: Because of the additional penalty that appears in \eqref{eq:pen} program, $d_{M}^\lambda(r,c)$ is necessarily larger than $d_M(r,c)$, and we expect this gap to decrease as $\lambda$ increases.
nodes.section: 5.2 Does the Sinkhorn Distance Converge to the EMD?
conclusions: $d_{M}^\lambda(r,c)$ is necessarily larger than $d_M(r,c)$
we expect this gap to decrease as $\lambda$ increases
nodes.statement_short: The entropic penalty makes $d_M^\lambda\ge d_M$, with the gap expected to shrink as $\lambda$ grows.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn distances stay about 10% above the EMD
nodes.statement: As can be observed, even with large values of $\lambda$, Sinkhorn distances hover above the values of EMD distances by about $10\%$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Does the Sinkhorn Distance Converge to the EMD?
conclusions: Sinkhorn distances hover above the values of EMD distances by about $10\%$

nodes.name: Speed-up over EMD solvers
nodes.statement: For large dimensions and on the same CPU, Sinkhorn distances are more than 100.000 faster than EMD solvers given a threshold of $0.01$.
assumptions: For large dimensions and on the same CPU
conclusions: Sinkhorn distances are more than 100.000 faster than EMD solvers given a threshold of $0.01$

nodes.name: Iterations grow with diagonal dominance
nodes.statement: As can be seen in Figure~\ref{fig:lambdacompt}, the number of iterations required so that $\norm{x-x'}_2\leq 0.01$ increases as $e^{-\lambda M}$ becomes diagonally dominant.
conclusions: the number of iterations required so that $\norm{x-x'}_2\leq 0.01$ increases as $e^{-\lambda M}$ becomes diagonally dominant

nodes.name: Proof of the Independence Kernel property
nodes.statement:
The set $U_1(r,c)$ contains all joint probabilities $P$ for which $h(P)=h(r)+h(c)$. In that case~\citep[Theorem 2.6.6]{cover91elements} applies and $U_1(r,c)$ can only be equal to the singleton $\{rc^T\}$. If $M$ is negative definite, there exists vectors $(\varphi_1,\cdots,\varphi_d)$ in some Euclidean space $\RR^n$ such that $m_{ij}=
orm{\varphi_i-\varphi_j}_2^2$ through \citep[\S3.3.2]{berg84harmonic}. We thus have that $$ egin{aligned}r^TM c&= \sum_{ij}r_i c_j 
orm{\varphi_i-\varphi_j}^2= (\sum_{i}r_i 
orm{\varphi_i}^2 + \sum_{i} c_i 
orm{\varphi_i}^2) - 2\sum_{ij} \dotprod{r_i\varphi_i}{c_j\varphi_j}\&= r^Tu + c^Tu - 2 r^TK c\end{aligned}$$ where $u_i=
orm{\phi_i}^2$ and $K_{ij}=\dotprod{\varphi_i}{\varphi_j}$. We used the fact that $\sum r_i=\sum c_i=1$ to go from the first to the second equality. $r^TMc$ is thus a n.d. kernel because it is the sum of two n.d. kernels: the first term $(r^Tu+c^Tu)$ is the sum of the same function evaluated separately on $r$ and $c$, and thus a negative definite kernel~\citep[\S3.2.10]{berg84harmonic}; the latter term $-2r^TKu$ is negative definite as minus a positive definite kernel~\citep[Definition \S3.1.1]{berg84harmonic}.
nodes.statement_short: At $\alpha=0$ the feasible set is $\{rc^T\}$; writing Euclidean $M$ via feature vectors splits $r^TMc$ into a sum of negative definite kernels.

nodes.name: Feasible set is the independence table
nodes.statement: The set $U_1(r,c)$ contains all joint probabilities $P$ for which $h(P)=h(r)+h(c)$. In that case~\citep[Theorem 2.6.6]{cover91elements} applies and $U_1(r,c)$ can only be equal to the singleton $\{rc^T\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $rc^T$ attains the entropy bound, so $U_1(r,c)=\{rc^T\}$.

nodes.name: Euclidean embedding
nodes.statement: If $M$ is negative definite, there exists vectors $(\varphi_1,\cdots,\varphi_d)$ in some Euclidean space $\RR^n$ such that $m_{ij}=\norm{\varphi_i-\varphi_j}_2^2$ through \citep[\S3.3.2]{berg84harmonic}.
nodes.statement_short: Represent $M$ through vectors $\varphi_i$.

nodes.name: Expand $r^TMc$
nodes.statement:
We thus have that $$ egin{aligned}r^TM c&= \sum_{ij}r_i c_j 
orm{\varphi_i-\varphi_j}^2= (\sum_{i}r_i 
orm{\varphi_i}^2 + \sum_{i} c_i 
orm{\varphi_i}^2) - 2\sum_{ij} \dotprod{r_i\varphi_i}{c_j\varphi_j}\&= r^Tu + c^Tu - 2 r^TK c\end{aligned}$$ where $u_i=
orm{\phi_i}^2$ and $K_{ij}=\dotprod{\varphi_i}{\varphi_j}$. We used the fact that $\sum r_i=\sum c_i=1$ to go from the first to the second equality.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $r^TMc$ into $r^Tu+c^Tu-2r^TKc$.

nodes.name: Sum of n.d. kernels
nodes.statement: $r^TMc$ is thus a n.d. kernel because it is the sum of two n.d. kernels: the first term $(r^Tu+c^Tu)$ is the sum of the same function evaluated separately on $r$ and $c$, and thus a negative definite kernel~\citep[\S3.2.10]{berg84harmonic}; the latter term $-2r^TKu$ is negative definite as minus a positive definite kernel~\citep[Definition \S3.1.1]{berg84harmonic}.
nodes.statement_short: Both terms are negative definite, hence so is $r^TMc$.

nodes.name: Fast computation of the Independence kernel
nodes.statement: The proof above suggests a faster way to compute the Independence kernel. Given a matrix $M$, one can indeed pre-compute the vector of norms $u$ as well as a Cholesky factor $L$ of $K$ above to preprocess a dataset of histograms by premultiplying each observations $r_i$ by $L$ and only store $Lr_i$ as well as precomputing its diagonal term $r_i^Tu$. Note that the independence kernel is positive definite on histograms with the same 1-norm, but is no longer positive definite for arbitrary vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Precomputing norms and a Cholesky factor of $K$ speeds up the independence kernel; it is p.d. only on equal-mass histograms.

nodes.name: Proof of the Gluing Lemma With Entropic Constraint
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the a probability distribution on $\{1,\cdots,d\}^d$ whose coefficients are defined as \begin{equation}t_{ijk}\defeq \frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j},\end{equation} for all indices $j$ such that $y_j>0$. For indices $j$ such that $y_j=0$, all values $t_{ijk}$ are set to $0$. Let $S \defeq [ \sum_{j} t_{ijk}]_{ik}$. $S$ is a transportation matrix between $x$ and $z$. Indeed, $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{i} \sum_{j} s_{ijk}&= \sum_{j} \sum_{i}\frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j}= \sum_{j} \frac{q_{jk}}{y_j} \sum_{i} p_{ij} =\sum_{j} \frac{q_{jk}}{y_j} y_j=\sum_j q_{jk}=z_k \text{ (column sums) }\\ \sum_{k} \sum_{j} s_{ijk}&= \sum_{j} \sum_{k}\frac{p_{ij}q_{jk}}{y_j}= \sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}}{y_j} \sum_{k}q_{jk} =\sum_{j} \frac{p_{ij}}{y_j} y_j=\sum_j p_{ij}=x_i \text{ (row sums) } \end{aligned} $$ We now prove that $h(S)\geq h(x)+h(z)-\alpha$. Let $(X,Y,Z)$ be three random variables jointly distributed as $T$. Since by definition of $T$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:T} $$p(X,Y,Z)=p(X,Y)p(Y,Z)/p(Y)= p(X)p(Y|X)p(Z|Y),$$ the triplet $(X,Y,Z)$ is a Markov chain $X\rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z$~\citep[Equation 2.118]{cover91elements} and thus, by virtue of the data processing inequality~\citep[Theorem 2.8.1]{cover91elements}, the following inequality between mutual informations applies: $$I(X;Y)\geq I(X;Z),\text{ namely } \quad h(X,Z)-h(X)+h(Z)\geq h(X,Y) -h(X)+h(Y)\geq -\alpha.$$
nodes.statement_short: Build the glued three-way table $T$, check its marginals, then bound the entropy of $S$ via the Markov chain and the data processing inequality.

nodes.statement_short: $S$ has row sums $x$ and column sums $z$.

nodes.statement: We now prove that $h(S)\geq h(x)+h(z)-\alpha$. Let $(X,Y,Z)$ be three random variables jointly distributed as $T$. Since by definition of $T$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:T} $$p(X,Y,Z)=p(X,Y)p(Y,Z)/p(Y)= p(X)p(Y|X)p(Z|Y),$$ the triplet $(X,Y,Z)$ is a Markov chain $X\rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z$~\citep[Equation 2.118]{cover91elements} and thus, by virtue of the data processing inequality~\citep[Theorem 2.8.1]{cover91elements}, the following inequality between mutual informations applies: $$I(X;Y)\geq I(X;Z),\text{ namely } \quad h(X,Z)-h(X)+h(Z)\geq h(X,Y) -h(X)+h(Y)\geq -\alpha.$$
nodes.statement_short: Prove $h(S)\ge h(x)+h(z)-\alpha$.
